title: Area IV review: Flight by Reference to Instruments
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area IV: attitude instrument flying and recovery from unusual attitudes. Many of them join the two in one real IFR situation, like a failure or an upset you must catch and fix on the instruments.

questions.q: You are at 90 knots true airspeed on a heading of 360. ATC says "turn right heading 090." About what bank gives a standard-rate turn, and at what heading do you start the roll-out?
options: About 9° of bank, rolling out near 085
About 14° of bank, rolling out near 076
About 14° of bank, rolling out near 083
About 18° of bank, rolling out near 081
questions.why: Standard-rate bank is about 15 percent of TAS: 90 ÷ 10 = 9, plus half of that (4.5) is about 14° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Lead the heading by half the bank, about 7°, so start the roll-out near 090 − 7 = 083 [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Rolling out at 076 would lead by the full bank angle.

questions.q: In IMC your panel looks like this. The attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator is level, the VSI reads zero and the altimeter is steady. Small red flags show on the attitude and heading indicators. What is the best response?
options: Fly level on the turn coordinator, VSI and altimeter, then tell ATC
Start an unusual attitude recovery from the left bank the attitude indicator shows
Roll right until the attitude indicator shows wings level, then check the others
Trust the attitude indicator, because it is the only direct bank instrument
questions.why: In this IFH figure the airplane is really level at 2,000 ft MSL, not turning left. A pilot who misses the failure flags can turn a harmless failure into a hazard [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI, fly with the instruments that still work, cover the failed ones if it helps, and advise ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

questions.q: In level cruise in rain with pitot heat off, the airspeed slowly drops toward zero. The altimeter is steady, the VSI reads zero, the attitude indicator shows level and the engine sounds normal. What is most likely?
options: The pitot tube is blocked with its drain hole open
The airplane is nose-high and slowing, so push forward now
The static ports are blocked, so airspeed reads low in cruise
The pitot tube and drain hole are both blocked, so airspeed is zero
questions.why: An odd reading means you speed up the cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or a malfunction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Here every other instrument shows level flight. With the pitot tube blocked and the drain hole open, indicated airspeed slowly drops to zero. If the drain hole were blocked too, the airspeed would act like an altimeter instead [[23:97|IFH 5-2]] [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

questions.q: Your PFD suddenly looks like this, and the airspeed is decreasing. There is no recovery procedure in the POH. Which recovery is right?
options: Level the wings, add power, then push forward to lower the nose
Add power, push forward to lower the nose, then level the wings
Push forward to lower the nose, level the wings, then reduce power
Reduce power, level the wings, then gently raise the nose
questions.why: Red chevrons point back to level pitch; pointing down to the horizon means nose-high [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With airspeed decreasing, increase power, apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose and prevent a stall, then level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, almost at once but in that order [[23:188|IFH 7-27]].

questions.q: After an unusual attitude recovery you are stable at 5,300 ft, assigned 6,000 ft. You climb back at 800 fpm, the best rate your airplane gives right now. At what altitude do you start the level-off?
questions.why: Once stable, return to the assigned altitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]]. The rate of return grows with the error but never exceeds the airplane's optimum climb rate [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Lead the level-off by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 10 percent of 800 fpm is 80 ft, so 6,000 − 80 = 5,920 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

questions.q: In IMC, halfway through a long standard-rate turn, you drop your pen and bend down quickly to grab it. As you look up, you feel the airplane rolling and tumbling in a new direction. What is this, and what do you do?
options: Somatogravic illusion: lower the nose a little until the feeling passes
The leans: roll toward the feeling until it fades, then check the instruments
Coriolis illusion: trust the instruments and keep head movement small
Attitude gyro failure: switch to partial panel and cover the attitude indicator
questions.why: An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create the illusion of rotation on an entirely different axis. The AIM calls it the most overwhelming of all illusions [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. A pilot who chases the feeling may maneuver into a dangerous attitude, so pick up dropped items with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: On a vectored climb at VY with climb power set, the airspeed has crept 5 knots below VY. Which instrument is primary for pitch, and what is the fix?
options: VSI: reduce power slightly to hold the climb rate
Airspeed indicator: lower the nose slightly
Altimeter: raise the nose slightly to climb faster
Attitude indicator: add power until VY returns
questions.why: Once a constant-airspeed climb is stable, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure is primary for power. If the attitude is right for the power set, airspeed settles at the target; if it is low or high, make a small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

questions.q: In a spiral dive you have pulled the throttle to idle, unloaded with some forward pressure and rolled the wings level. The airspeed is now at the red line. What next?
options: Raise the nose gently to level, then climb when speed is safe
Add climb power right away and pull up firmly to a climb attitude
Push forward more to unload until the airspeed is well below the red line
Pull firmly to level flight before the speed builds past the red line
questions.why: The airplane may be at or beyond VNE, so raise the nose to level flight slowly and gently to prevent structural failure. Raise it to a climb attitude only after the speed is safe, and add climb power once the airspeed is at VY [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: Leveling off at 7,000 ft, you stare at the VSI trying to hold it exactly on zero. Meanwhile the heading drifts 15° and the airspeed climbs past cruise. What error is this, and what is the fix?
options: Omission: add the VSI to your scan more often
Emphasis: lean on the attitude indicator for pitch
Overcontrol: grip the yoke tighter so pitch can't change
Fixation: break the stare and cross-check every instrument
questions.why: Fixation is staring at one instrument; the IFH example shows the heading wandering while the pilot stares [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Chasing the VSI is a common error, fixed by cross-checking the other pitch instruments [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. In a level-off at cruise you also reduce power as airspeed nears cruise, which the stare made you miss [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

questions.q: You are single pilot in IMC with light turbulence. ATC gives you a long reroute to load into the GPS. Your autopilot works well. What is the best plan?
options: Engage the autopilot, then program the GPS while you monitor the flight
Hand fly to stay sharp, and program between glances at the panel
Refuse the reroute, since programming a GPS in IMC is too risky
Trim carefully, then program it heads-down; the airplane will hold itself
questions.why: Use the autopilot to reduce workload; it gives you more time to monitor the flight and lowers the chance of entering an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Preoccupation with flight deck duties and a careless cross-check are listed causes of unusual attitudes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: After a vacuum failure you steer by the magnetic compass. Near 35° N latitude, you turn left from west to south with about 16° of bank. Using the IFH rule, at what compass reading do you start the roll-out?
options: About 153°
About 145°
About 207°
About 188°
questions.why: With 15° to 18° of bank, the lead or lag for north and south turns is about your latitude. Turning to south, hold the turn until the compass passes south by the latitude, minus the normal roll-out lead of half the bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. From the west: 180 − 35 + 8 = 153°. The IFH example at 30° gives 157° from the west [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; 207° would be the answer when turning from the east.

questions.q: You look up from a chart in IMC and find a steep, nose-low bank with the airspeed building fast. You are about 4,000 ft above the ground. How should you size your control inputs?
options: As large and fast as you can, since every second counts
Very small, waiting several seconds between each input
In proportion to the size and rate of the upset
Full back pressure first, then deal with the bank
questions.why: Control inputs and power changes should be in direct proportion to the amount and rate of change of roll, yaw, pitch or airspeed, so you don't overstress the airplane, unless ground contact is imminent [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. Pulling back first is the instinctive, wrong reaction in a nose-low attitude [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

questions.q: You are descending at 500 fpm and 90 knots to 3,000 ft, and you want to stay at 90 knots once level. When and how do you level off?
options: At 3,150 ft: add cruise power and hold forward pressure
At 3,000 ft: level the nose, then add power as speed drops
At 3,100 ft: level the nose and leave the descent power set
At 3,050 ft: level the nose and add power to hold 90 knots
questions.why: To level off at descent airspeed, lead the altitude by about 50 ft, level the pitch attitude and add power to a setting that holds the airspeed constant, then trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The 100 to 150 ft lead is for leveling off at a speed higher than descent speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

questions.q: Before your instrument rating, you fly VFR into cloud by mistake. ATC says the bases are lower and suggests you descend to get below them. By the AFH, how do you descend?
options: Pull the power to idle and hold the nose level until you break out
Lower the nose two bar widths and keep cruise power so you get out of the cloud fast
Make a gentle descending turn back toward the clear area behind you
Reduce power in small steps, wings level, 500 fpm max, one bar down
questions.why: With the airplane trimmed, reduce power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch of manifold pressure. The descent should never exceed 500 fpm, the wings stay level and pitch stays within one bar width below level [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. An untrained instrument pilot should avoid combined maneuvers such as descending turns [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

questions.q: In a glass-panel airplane like the IFH example, the AHRS fails in IMC while the air data computer keeps working. What do you lose?
options: The airspeed and altitude tapes, while attitude and heading remain
Only the heading display; attitude and the autopilot keep working
Attitude, heading, upset protection, and most autopilot modes
Everything on the PFD, so only the magnetic compass is left
questions.why: An AHRS failure removes all heading and attitude indications from the PFD and all unusual attitude protection. All autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost too [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. With air data still working, the altimeter and VSI tapes remain [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

questions.q: You blunder into an embedded thunderstorm with the autopilot's altitude hold and speed hold on. The turbulence is heavy. What should you do with the autopilot?
options: Leave both modes on so the autopilot fights the drafts for you
Disengage altitude hold and speed hold, since they add stress
Switch altitude hold off but keep speed hold to protect VNE
Disconnect it and turn around to fly back out of the storm
questions.why: Altitude hold and speed hold only increase the airplane's maneuvering and the structural stress, so disengage them. Hold a level attitude at turbulence penetration speed and fly straight through; turning only adds stress [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

questions.q: Your attitude and heading indicators have failed. How do you trim for hands-off straight flight using the turn coordinator?
options: Center the ball with aileron, level the miniature airplane with rudder
Trim nose-up until the VSI is zero, then center the ball with aileron
Level the miniature airplane with aileron, center the ball with rudder
Use rudder trim toward the side away from the ball until it centers
questions.why: Use aileron pressure to level the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft and rudder pressure to center the ball. Hold them, then release them slowly while you add rudder trim to relieve the rudder pressure [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Rudder trim goes toward the side the ball is displaced [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

questions.q: You recover from a long nose-low left turn. The turn coordinator now shows wings level with the ball centered, but you strongly feel banked to the right. What should you do?
options: Roll slightly left until the feeling of a right bank goes away
Hold wings level on the instruments and ignore the feeling
Trust the feeling and assume the turn coordinator has failed
Close your eyes for a moment to sense the real attitude of the airplane
questions.why: After a long turn, rolling out makes you feel a turn the opposite way, and a disoriented pilot may roll back into the original turn [[23:72|IFH 3-5]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Disorientation can be prevented only by fixed outside references or the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]], so trust the instruments and disregard your sensations [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

questions.q: You are level at your assigned 7,000 ft and the altimeter is steady, but the airspeed is 10 knots slow. The manifold pressure is 2 inches below your usual cruise setting. What do you do?
options: Lower the nose to regain the airspeed, then climb back up
Add power to the cruise setting and hold the level attitude
Lower the nose slightly and leave the power where it is
Raise the nose, since low airspeed means you are descending
questions.why: Before deciding on a power change, always check the altimeter [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Altitude is right and power is low, so power is the fix. Pushing forward for low airspeed when a low power setting is the cause is a common pitch error [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

questions.q: You practice unusual attitude recoveries under a view-limiting device with a friend as safety pilot. What collision risk does AC 90-48E warn safety pilots about?
options: Radar advisories make it safe for both pilots to watch the panel during recoveries
Only the hooded pilot needs to clear the area before each recovery
Traffic is not a concern while the airplane is above 3,000 ft AGL in practice areas
Safety pilots tend to look inside too much and forget see and avoid
questions.why: Safety pilots and instructors should be especially alert during simulated instrument flight, where there is a tendency to look inside excessively and forget see-and-avoid [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]. The IFH gives a good setup for this kind of practice in its stall section: a safe altitude, an area free of conflicting traffic and radar traffic advisories [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: Right after a nose-high recovery, the turn coordinator shows wings level but the ball is off to the left. What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: A skid: add left rudder to center the ball, then retrim
A slip: add right rudder to center the ball, then retrim
A skid: add right aileron until the ball is centered
A slip: lower the left wing until the ball is centered
questions.why: Wings level with the ball off center is a skid. Center the ball with rudder on the ball's side (left ball, left rudder), use aileron for bank and retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. In a recovery the ball must be centered, because slipping and skidding sensations make disorientation worse [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

questions.q: In IMC near building cumulus, a strong updraft hits. You feel a climb, and the altimeter jumps 300 ft in a few seconds, but the attitude indicator shows level. What should you do?
options: Push the nose down firmly to hold the assigned altitude on the altimeter
Reduce power to idle and follow the altimeter back down
Raise the nose, since the climb will soon bleed off airspeed
Hold level attitude on the attitude indicator; let altitude vary
questions.why: An updraft can create the elevator illusion of a climb, and the disoriented pilot pushes nose-low [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The altimeter is not a good pitch reference in exceptionally strong vertical currents such as thunderstorms [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. In storm turbulence, hold a level attitude and let airspeed and altitude fluctuate [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].
